author: Amphilochius of Iconium
addressee: A Christian congregation, with heretics as the opponents addressed
occasion: A homily against heretics who use Christ's prayer “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” to claim that the Son is fearful, needy, and inferior to the Father.
argument: Amphilochius opens by presenting himself as a soldier fighting heretics under the martyr Stephen's protection. He then voices the heretics' objections: if Christ is life and resurrection, why does he fear death and pray to avoid it? In response, Christ himself is made to explain that his fear is a deliberate stratagem: he hides his divinity and displays human weakness so that the devil and death will attack him as a mere man and be defeated. The homily concludes that the flesh suffered while the divine Word remained impassible, and that the Father neither lacked power nor withheld mercy in not removing the cup.

outline.move: Amphilochius announces his battle against heretics, invokes the martyr Stephen's aid, and asks Christ to interpret his own words against those who charge him with fear and inferiority.
Christ answers the heretics' objections: he declares he does not fear death, explaining that he willingly took on passible flesh to grant life through death, undoing Adam's condemnation.
Christ continues his answer: he willingly took a passible body and accepted death to undo Adam's condemnation, fulfilling the law as man and granting resurrection through baptism.
Christ explains that his apparent fear is bait: by hiding his divinity and showing human weakness, he deceives the devil into attacking him, so that the devil is caught on the hook of divinity.
Christ continues: he conquers through weakness, not power, so that victory is credited to human nature; the devil's own weapon, death, becomes the source of resurrection.
Christ is both shepherd and sheep: he hides his divinity as shepherd and offers his flesh as sheep, so that the devil seizes the flesh and is slain by the Spirit's sword.
Christ argues that the flesh, not the impassible Word, suffered; he warns that denying this makes the Father either powerless or cruel, and ironically makes the Son stronger than the Father.

The homily concludes that Christ only seemed to fear, in order to deceive the devil; descending to Hades he plundered it invisibly, and the doxology is offered to Christ with the Father and the Spirit.

cast.name: Amphilochius of Iconium
cast.who: The preacher and bishop who delivers the homily against heretics.

cast.name: Stephen
cast.who: The protomartyr Stephen, invoked as the general of piety whose prayer aids Amphilochius in battle.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: The divine Word incarnate, who speaks in the first person through much of the homily to explain his prayer and passion.

cast.name: Moses
cast.who: Old Testament lawgiver, cited as an example of prayer aiding victory in battle.

cast.name: Joshua
cast.who: Old Testament leader who defeated enemies while Moses prayed.

cast.name: Eunomius
cast.who: Heretic named as rejoicing over Christ's words, representing those who charge the Son with fear.

cast.name: Arius
cast.who: Heretic named alongside Eunomius as seizing Christ's words as material for blasphemy.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: The apostle who tried to dissuade Christ from the passion and was rebuked as Satan.

cast.name: Hosea
cast.who: Prophet cited as foretelling deliverance from Hades and victory over death.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: Apostle cited on God's knowledge of all creation.

cast.name: Lazarus
cast.who: The man Christ raised from the dead, cited as proof of his power over death.

cast.name: Jairus's daughter
cast.who: The girl Christ raised, cited as proof of his power over death.

cast.name: The widow's son
cast.who: The young man Christ raised at Nain, cited as proof of his power over death.

cast.name: Adam
cast.who: The first man, whose sin brought death and whose condemnation Christ reverses.

cast.name: The devil
cast.who: The deceiver and tyrant who brought death through Adam and is deceived and defeated by Christ's apparent weakness.

cast.name: Isaiah
cast.who: Prophet cited as witness that Christ's garments, not his divine nature, were stained with blood.

cast.name: Jacob
cast.who: Patriarch cited as prophesying the washing of Christ's garment (his body) in wine and his wrap in the blood of the grape.

cast.name: Apollinaris
cast.who: Heretic whose error taught that Christ took a body without a soul, refuted by Christ's troubled soul.

cast.name: Job
cast.who: Old Testament figure cited for the prophecy of drawing the dragon with a hook.

voices.speaker: Amphilochius
voices.how_marked: The preacher's own voice, opening and closing the homily and addressing the heretics directly.

voices.speaker: Christ
voices.how_marked: Introduced as the one asked to interpret his own words; speaks in the first person, often marked by verbs of saying such as φησίν.

voices.speaker: Heretics (quoted objections)
voices.how_marked: Their objections are paraphrased or quoted as questions and charges against Christ, sometimes introduced by φασίν or νομίζουσιν.

voices.speaker: Scripture (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Quotations from the prophets, apostles, and Gospel are introduced by formulas such as λέγων, φησίν, or γέγραπται.

key_terms.sense: God's saving plan, especially the incarnation and passion as a deliberate arrangement for human salvation.
The apparent fear or timidity Christ displays as part of his strategy to deceive the devil.
Deception, both the devil's original deception of Adam and Christ's counter-deception of the devil.
The human flesh or body Christ assumed, the passible element in which he suffers and dies.
Christ's divine nature, which remains impassible and hidden during the passion.
The divine Word, the Son of God, who becomes flesh and remains impassible.
The passion, Christ's suffering and death on the cross.
Death, personified as the enemy Christ defeats and as the penalty for Adam's sin.
Resurrection, Christ's rising and the rising of the dead he accomplishes.
Sin, the transgression that brought death into the world through Adam.
The cup of suffering and death Christ prays to have pass from him.
The hook of Christ's divinity, baited with his flesh, by which the devil is caught.
The bait, Christ's human weakness and fear, used to lure the devil and death.
The heretics who misinterpret Christ's prayer and charge him with fear and inferiority.
The devil as tyrant who held humanity in bondage through sin and death.

scripture: The author uses Septuagint book names and Psalm numbering. Hosea is cited as Ὠσηὲ (Hosea). The Psalms are cited according to the Septuagint numbering; modern citations should use the corresponding Hebrew numbering where they differ. New Testament quotations follow the Gospels and Pauline epistles. Citations should be given in modern form, e.g., 'Hosea 13:14' for the quotation from Hosea, and 'Psalm 16:10' for 'You will not let your holy one see corruption' (LXX Psalm 15:10).
uncertain: The exact date of the homily is not stated in the source.
The precise occasion or liturgical setting is not specified beyond the anti-heretical purpose.
The identity of the heretics is not limited to Eunomius and Arius; they are named as examples, and the broader target may include other groups.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: u02-rem-mid: 'Μὴ τὰ πάθη οὖν τῆς σαρκὸς τῷ ἀπαθεῖ προσρίψῃς λόγῳ· θεὸς γάρ εἰμι καὶ ἄνθρωπος, αἱρετικέ. Θεὸς ὡς ἐγγυᾶται τὰ θαύματα, ἄνθρωπος ὡς μαρτυρεῖ τὰ παθήματα.' u02-rem-close: 'Ἀλλὰ μὴ γένοιτο! Οὔτε γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ ἢ ἀφειδῶν ἢ ἀδυναμῶν οὐκ ἠλευθέρωσέν με τοῦ πάθους, οὔτε ἐγὼ παραιτούμενος τὸ πάθος ᾔτησα παρελθεῖν τὸ ποτήριον.'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The voice in u02-rem-mid and u02-rem-close is Christ speaking in the first person, not Amphilochius. Amphilochius's voice appears only in u01-open and the brief doxology at the very end of u02-rem-close ('Καὶ ταῦτα μὲν οὕτως. Ὑπὲρ δὲ τῶν εἰρημένων δόξαν ἀναπέμψωμεν...').

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: u01-rem-early: 'Ἐν σοί ἐστιν ἢ καταδέξασθαι ἢ παραιτήσασθαι τὸ πάθος. Εἰ δὲ οὐκ ἐν σοὶ κεῖται, εἰκότως δειλιᾷς ὡς ἄκων καὶ παρὰ γνώμην ἐπὶ τὸ πάθος ἑλκόμενος...'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The objections continue throughout u01-rem-early and extend into u01-rem-mid and u01-rem-close. The heretics' objections are voiced as rhetorical questions addressed to Christ through much of the first half of the homily, not just in u01-open and u01-rem-early.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Jacob: 'Patriarch cited as prophesying the washing of Christ's garment (his body) in wine and his wrap in the blood of the grape.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: u02-rem-early: 'Μάρτυς δὲ καὶ Ἰακὼβ ὁ πατριάρχης ὁ περὶ ἐμοῦ λέγων· Πλυνεῖ ἐν οἴνῳ τὴν στολὴν αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐν αἵματι σταφυλῆς τὴν περιβολὴν αὐτοῦ. Ποίαν στολήν; τὸ σῶμα. Ποίῳ αἵματι; τῷ ἐκ τῆς πλευρᾶς ῥεύσαντι.'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source identifies this as Jacob (Ἰακὼβ ὁ πατριάρχης), but the quotation 'Πλυνεῖ ἐν οἴνῳ τὴν στολὴν αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐν αἵματι σταφυλῆς τὴν περιβολὴν αὐτοῦ' is from Genesis 49:11, which is a prophecy of Jacob/Israel about Judah, not a self-referential prophecy by Jacob about himself. The brief's description is slightly misleading; Jacob is cited as the speaker of the prophecy, not as the one prophesied about.

_unresolved_facts.claim: u01-rem-early move: 'Christ answers the heretics' objections: he declares he does not fear death, explaining that he willingly took on passible flesh to grant life through death, undoing Adam's condemnation.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: u01-rem-early contains extensive heretic objections before Christ's answer: 'Ἐν σοί ἐστιν ἢ καταδέξασθαι ἢ παραιτήσασθαι τὸ πάθος...' through 'ματαία ἡμῶν ἡ ἐλπίς, ἀνόνητος ἡ προσδοκία.'
_unresolved_facts.fix: u01-rem-early contains both extended heretic objections AND Christ's initial answer. The move should note that this section continues the dialectical format with objections before turning to Christ's explanation.

_unresolved_facts.claim: u01-rem-mid move: 'Christ continues his answer: he willingly took a passible body and accepted death to undo Adam's condemnation, fulfilling the law as man and granting resurrection through baptism.'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The description is accurate but incomplete. u01-rem-mid also contains the extended discussion of Christ as master of nature who operates beyond nature's order, with the analogy of sun/moon/fire/water, and the statement that Christ knows how the incarnation works but the listener cannot understand it.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The homily concludes that 'the Father neither lacked power nor withheld mercy in not removing the cup.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: u02-rem-close: 'Οὔτε γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ ἢ ἀφειδῶν ἢ ἀδυναμῶν οὐκ ἠλευθέρωσέν με τοῦ πάθους, οὔτε ἐγὼ παραιτούμενος τὸ πάθος ᾔτησα παρελθεῖν τὸ ποτήριον.'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The conclusion is more precisely that the Father did not fail to free Christ from suffering either through lack of mercy (ἀφειδῶν) or inability (ἀδυναμῶν), AND that Christ did not ask to avoid the passion out of genuine fear but as a stratagem. The brief's phrasing 'withheld mercy' slightly misrepresents ἀφειδῶν (being sparing/harsh).

_unresolved_facts.claim: The devil: 'The deceiver and tyrant who brought death through Adam and is deceived and defeated by Christ's apparent weakness.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: u01-rem-close: 'Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ εἶδεν ὁ διάβολος... φοβεῖται καὶ δέδιεν σταυρῷ με προσηλῶσαι καὶ θανάτῳ παραδοῦναι, ἵνα μὴ νεκροῦ ὑπεισελθὼν σχῆμα τοὺς νεκροὺς ἐλευθερώσω.'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source does not explicitly state that the devil 'brought death through Adam.' The devil deceived Adam, and death came through sin, but the causal chain is more nuanced in the text. The devil is called τύραννος who 'found sin and through sin introduced death' (τὴν ἁμαρτίαν εὑρὼν καὶ διὰ τῆς ἁμαρτίας τὸν θάνατον εἰσαγαγὼν), but this is in Christ's speech about the devil's actions, not a direct claim that the devil himself brought death.
